title: The Church in Your House
subtitle: Philemon 1:1–7
description: The letter arrives with Onesimus himself: Paul greets Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the church in Philemon's house, and gives thanks for a love that refreshes the saints.
paragraphs: This letter did not travel alone. When Paul sent word to the church at Colossae, the same two men carried a second, much smaller letter to one house in the same city. Tychicus carried the news, and with him walked Onesimus, and this short letter is about Onesimus. It is the most personal thing Paul ever wrote that has come down to us: not an argument to a church, not a warning against false teaching, but a request from one man to another, about a third man who was traveling with the letter itself. One chapter, twenty-five verses, and it opens the way every letter of Paul opens, with the names.

The greeting names four recipients, and together they describe a household. It begins, “Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our beloved fellow worker.” Paul does not introduce himself as an apostle here, as he does to churches. He introduces himself as a prisoner, and the man he writes to first is a partner: Philemon, a believer of Colossae whose love and work Paul already knows and thanks God for. After him comes the family and the flock in one breath: “to Apphia our sister, to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church that meets at your house.” A sister, a soldier, and a whole church gathered under Philemon's roof. The request Paul is about to make belongs to all of them, because the man it concerns will walk back into that room. Then the blessing every letter carries: “Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

Before Paul asks for anything, he gives thanks, and the thanks is specific. “I always thank my God, remembering you in my prayers,” he writes, “because I hear about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints.” Word about Philemon travels. Reports of this man's faith toward the Lord and his love toward God's people have reached a prison cell in another country, and Paul has been carrying Philemon in his prayers on the strength of them. Then Paul tells him what he prays: “your partnership in the faith may become effective as you fully acknowledge every good thing that is ours in Christ.” Partnership is the word to hold onto. Paul is not writing to a stranger he hopes to persuade. He is writing to a partner, a man already sharing in the work, and praying that the sharing will grow fuller and more active. The request coming later in this letter will land on ground this prayer has already prepared.

And the thanks rests on something the whole church at Colossae could see. “I take great joy and encouragement in your love,” Paul writes, “because you, brother, have refreshed the hearts of the saints.” Refreshed is the word the letter will use again at its climax, when Paul asks Philemon to refresh his own heart. For now it describes what Philemon already does: tired and burdened believers come away from this man rested. His house is a church, his table is open, and his love is the kind that other people's hearts recover inside of. That is the man Paul is about to ask for the hardest thing he ever asked a friend: to receive back, as a brother, a slave who had been separated from him, and to let the whole watching household see him do it.

So the letter opens with joy, prayer, and a reputation, and it has not yet named its subject. Onesimus is not mentioned until verse 10. Paul spends his first seven verses standing in front of Philemon's whole household, thanking God for the man's love, in a room where that love is a matter of record. Everything the appeal needs is already on the table: a prisoner writing, a partner reading, a church listening in its own meeting place. What Paul asks next, he will ask on the basis of love, and he has begun by showing that love is the one currency this house already deals in.

title: I Appeal to You for My Child Onesimus
subtitle: Philemon 1:8–16
description: Paul could command and instead appeals on the basis of love, for his child Onesimus, formerly useless and now useful, sent back no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother.
paragraphs: Paul has spent seven verses giving thanks. Now the letter turns, and it turns carefully, because Paul begins by naming the road he is not taking. He has authority here, and he says so: “in Christ I am bold enough to order you to do what is proper.” Philemon owes the faith his obedience, and Paul, an apostle writing to a fellow worker, could simply command what ought to be done and expect it done. The whole appeal that follows only has its force because that road stood open. Paul closes it himself: “I prefer to appeal on the basis of love.” Not an order laid on a subordinate, but a request laid before a friend, from a man with no leverage left except the truth about himself: “I, Paul, am now aged, and a prisoner of Christ Jesus as well.” An old man, in chains, asking.

Then, at verse 10, the letter finally names its subject, and the naming is a claim all by itself: “I appeal to you for my child Onesimus, whose father I became while I was in chains.” Onesimus was Philemon's slave. Somewhere between Colossae and Paul's prison, the separated slave and the apostle met, and Paul led him to Christ, and now he calls him his child. Whatever Onesimus had been in Philemon's house, in Paul's cell he had become family. And Paul does not hide the history in the new name. He plays on the man's own name, which means useful, and lets the wordplay carry the story: “Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me.” Useless to Philemon, useful now to Paul in his chains, and the letter is traveling back with him so that he can become useful to Philemon again, in a way neither of them has yet seen.

What Paul is doing, he states with a plainness that must have cost him: “I am sending back to you him who is my very heart.” He is not keeping Onesimus. A beloved helper, a son in the faith, the one bright usefulness in a prisoner's days, and Paul packs him onto the road to Colossae with Tychicus, because the man does not belong to Paul. He belongs, in the arrangement of that world, to Philemon, and Paul will not build his own comfort on another man's household. He admits the wish he is refusing: “I would have liked to keep him with me, so that on your behalf he could minister to me in my chains for the gospel.” Even the keeping would have been framed as Philemon's own service, Onesimus standing in for his master at the prisoner's side. Paul wanted it. He would not take it.

The reason is the hinge of the whole letter: “I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will.” Paul could have presented Philemon with a settled fact, a converted slave already installed in the apostle's service, and dared him to object. Instead he returns the decision to the man it belongs to, because a goodness extracted by pressure is not the goodness he is asking for. Philemon must choose this freely or it is not the thing Paul wants at all. The prisoner who cannot leave his cell is protecting the freedom of the man who can do anything he likes. That is the shape of the appeal: authority held back, consent honored, and the whole matter placed in the hands of the one person with the legal power to crush it.

Then Paul reaches for the largest frame he can put around the separation, and he reaches gently, with a perhaps: “perhaps this is why he was separated from you for a while, so that you might have him back for good.” Separated: the letter never says Onesimus ran, never says he stole, never tells us how a slave of Colossae came to be sitting in a prisoner's room in another country. Paul does not fill in the gap, and neither does this telling. What Paul says is that the separation, however it happened, may have had a purpose inside it: a brief loss exchanged for a permanent return. And he names what is coming back through Philemon's door: “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother.” Not a slave improved or a slave forgiven his place, but a brother, and then the sentence leans in: “He is especially beloved to me, but even more so to you, both in person and in the Lord.” More to Philemon than to Paul. The man who owned him is asked to receive him as the one who loves him most.

title: Charge That to My Account
subtitle: Philemon 1:17–25
description: Receive him as you would receive me: Paul signs the debt note in his own hand, asks Philemon to refresh his heart, and closes with a guest room and greetings.
paragraphs: The appeal now becomes a transaction, and Paul conducts it in the open, with the whole household listening. It starts with the word the first episode planted: partner. “if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me.” Partnership in the faith, prayed over in verse 6, is now called in. If Paul and Philemon truly share in the work, then Philemon's door must open to Onesimus exactly as wide as it would open to Paul himself. Not a lesser welcome for a lesser man. The same welcome. Receive him as you would receive me is the sentence the whole letter has been walking toward, and it leaves no room for a halfway mercy, a pardon that keeps the man at the back of the house. The partner's child, the partner's very heart, is to be received as the partner.

Then Paul takes the last obstacle onto his own ledger. A returning slave might owe his master more than an apology; the letter never itemizes it, and neither does this telling. Paul simply covers it, whatever it is: “if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account.” And he signs the note like a man who knows exactly what a signature means: “I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it.” The letter, written out by another hand as Paul's letters usually were, takes its pen into Paul's own fingers for the promise, so that Philemon would see the name written by the prisoner himself. Only then comes the gentlest pressure in the letter, one clause long: “not to mention that you owe me your very self.” Philemon's own life in Christ came to him through Paul. The account between these two men was never going to balance, and both of them know it, and Paul mentions it only to leave it unmentioned.

What Paul wants for himself, out of all of it, he asks in the letter's own favorite word: “let me have some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ.” Refreshed is what Philemon does. The hearts of the saints have been refreshed through him, Paul said at the start, and now the prisoner asks for his share: refresh mine. Do this thing, receive this brother, and an old man in chains on the other side of the world will rest easier for it. And Paul writes as a man who already knows the answer. “Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I ask.” More than I ask: the letter never spells out what the more could be. It leaves the door of that sentence standing open, the way Paul leaves the decision standing open, for Philemon to walk through in a direction even the apostle only hints at.

The ending looks past the request entirely, to a visit. “prepare a guest room for me, because I hope that through your prayers I will be restored to you.” Paul expects to be released, expects to travel, expects to sleep under Philemon's roof, in the house where the church meets, where Onesimus will by then be living as a brother. The guest room is a quiet masterpiece of an ending for an appeal: Paul will come and see. Not to inspect, as far as the letter says, but the man who receives Onesimus will one day receive Paul at the same door, and both receptions will say what this household believes. Then the greetings gather the circle one last time: “Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings,” and “as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers.” The man who taught Colossae the gospel, the cousin of Barnabas, the beloved physician: the same small company that stands around the Colossians letter stands around this one. And over a slave owner, the slave he sent home, and a church in a house, Paul writes the last line he writes over all of them: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.”

The letter does not record what Philemon did. It ends, and the answer was given not in ink but in a doorway in Colossae, when a church that met in a man's house watched him receive the letter, and receive the man who carried it home. Scripture lets the appeal stand as the record. But the letter survived, copied and kept and read by the churches, and a request that failed would have been a strange thing to preserve. What we know is what Paul knew when he wrote: the hearts of the saints had been refreshed through Philemon before. The prisoner signed his name, sent his heart back up the road, and waited to hear whether it happened again. With this letter the prison writings close: four letters from one man's chains, to two churches, one friend across the sea, and one household, and the chains, in the end, carried further than the man who wore them.
